title: What the parties say about the draft
question: Should Haredi yeshiva students be drafted?

stances.label: Raise Haredi service step by step

note: Party answers to Ynet's September 2026 questionnaire unless another source is given. Likud declined the questionnaire; its stance comes from a minister's description of the coalition's 2025 bill. Ra'am answered only on drafting Arab citizens. Blue and White's row is from Ynet's Hebrew report of the same questionnaire. No 2026 position found for Noam (checked October 2026); its row gives Maoz's position in 2025.

rows.text: "Likud chose not to respond to inquiries from ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth regarding the draft law." In July 2025, Communications Minister Shlomo Karhi said the coalition was "fighting here for a historic conscription law that will conscript about 17,000 young Haredi men within three years."
rows.source: Ynet, Sep 16, 2026; Times of Israel, Jul 23, 2025

rows.text: Ynet's summary of its answer: "Shas acknowledges that it will no longer be possible to avoid drafting yeshiva students who have left their studies."

Ynet's summary: both factions "continue to oppose the enlistment of students who have dropped out of yeshivas" and oppose a universal draft law. The party "says the law it seeks to pass is intended solely to regulate the status of those who study Torah."

"Passing a Basic Law for Service Members under the principle of 'first in equality' — those who serve receive everything." Supports "expanding the pool of those who serve"; did not answer the question on sanctions.

Party leader Ben-Gvir: "We opened dedicated tracks in the police and Border Police, with full observance of Shabbat, kashrut, prayers and Torah study, appropriate gender separation and the establishment of the ultra-Orthodox 'Avnet' company in the Border Police."
Party leader Winter: "We will not join a government that does not pass, before it is formed, a law that puts an end to draft evasion and requires everyone to report for service… Full stop."

National service for all; the "only mechanism for deferring service will be an allocation of up to 3% of each annual cohort for outstanding individuals." Eisenkot puts that at about 2,200 a year of a 70,000-person national cohort (all Israelis, not Haredim only), and would "revoke any state incentives granted to those who evade service."
"Every citizen… will enlist in the IDF or perform national civilian service… without exemptions — that applies to Arabs and to the ultra-Orthodox alike."
"The obligation to serve the state should apply to all citizens, within a national and equal framework."
"Every young man and woman at age 18 — Jews, Muslims, Christians, Druze and Circassians — will be required to perform military or civilian service. No exemptions, no quotas and no deals."

"Every citizen will report to the induction center." Those who do not serve would face "revocation of a driver's license, a ban on leaving the country, exclusion from public-sector and government jobs," and loss of tax, housing and daycare benefits.
Ynet reports that it opposes drafting Haredi men or any form of compulsory enlistment. The party: "sanctions should not be imposed on someone who chooses not to enlist."
Ynet reports that it opposes a draft law that would require young Arab citizens to serve in the IDF or perform civilian service, and that it declined to respond on Haredi enlistment.

No 2026 position found. In December 2025, the Times of Israel reported that Avi Maoz supports more Haredi service but would back only a noncoercive bill with Haredi rabbinic approval, and would not say how he would vote.

"A service framework for all: every young man and woman will serve the state," Haredim, Arabs, Druze, religious and secular. The framework must pass "before the government is formed as a condition for its swearing-in"; quotas replace targets, so "only outstanding individuals will receive exemptions"; benefits go first to those who serve (translated).
